list.listitem: Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) is an important consideration in a patient presenting with asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss. C
Use auditory brainstem response (ABR) audiometry for the initial evaluation; however, if the index of suspicion is high, gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the gold standard diagnostic test. C
Treatment options include surgery, stereotactic radiosurgery, radiation, and in some cases, observation. B
A multidisciplinary evaluation by an experienced neurotologic surgeon and radiation oncologist is recommended. C

background.definition: Acoustic neuroma (also called vestibular schwannoma) is a benign Schwann cell-derived tumor commonly originating from the vestibular portion of the eighth cranial nerve.

list.listitem: Occurs in about 1 per 100,000 person years.
Account for approximately 8% of intracranial tumors in adults.
Incidence increases with age and is highest in the 45- to 64-year-old age group.
It is the most common tumor of the cerebellopontine angle.
Tumors are unilateral in more than 90% of patients.
Type 2 neurofibromatosis (NF2) is characterized by the presence of bilateral vestibular schwannomas.
Five percent to 10% of vestibular schwannomas are diagnosed in patients with NF2.
In most cases, the cause of developing vestibular schwannoma is unknown.
The only well-established risk factor for diagnosis of vestibular schwannoma is a personal or family history of NF2.

Data associating noise exposure with vestibular schwannoma are conflicting and associations are weak at best. The risk is somewhat lower among ever or current smokers than never smokers (OR 0.53, 95% CI 0.30-0.94).
Exposure to radiofrequency energy from long-term cellular telephone usage as a risk factor is controversial and a subject of current investigation.
Vestibular schwannomas arise from the perineural Schwann cells.
Malignant degeneration is extremely rare.
Vestibular schwannomas are slow growing. Growth typically occurs at less than 3 mm per year, and some may not grow at all.

Vestibular schwannoma is a rare cause of asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss. It typically presents with a gradual onset and is sometimes associated with deficits of the facial and trigeminal nerves as well. B
ABR audiometry can be used as a screening tool. C
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the gold standard diagnostic test. A

Differential.Differential_Features: Onset of hearing loss is typically sudden
Symptoms are episodic, more frequently associated with vertigo
Usually bilateral, often part of an overall systemic autoimmune problem

list.listitem: More than 90% of patients typically present with unilateral hearing loss as the principal complaint. Hearing loss is usually gradually progressive, and the diagnosis is made after an average of 3.7 years of diminished hearing.
Tinnitus and dysequilibrium are also common complaints.

The external and middle ear appear normal on physical examination. Deficits in the ipsilateral trigeminal and facial nerves can be identified on physical examination in a minority of patients. An absent corneal reflex may be detected when cranial nerve V also becomes affected.
The Rinne and Weber tests can be used to confirm sensorineural hearing loss.

Only 5% of patients with asymmetric sensorineural hearing loss or unilateral tinnitus are found to have an abnormality on MRI that can account for their symptoms, and only 1% are diagnosed with an acoustic neuroma.
Pure tone and speech audiometry can be used as a screening test in patients presenting with new complaints of unilateral hearing loss or tinnitus.
ABR audiometry can be used for further screening in patients with unexplained asymmetries. Sensitivity is 92% overall but declines with smaller tumors (83% for tumors <1.0 cm).
Gadolinium-enhanced MRI is the gold standard diagnostic test. Include thin cuts through the internal auditory canal.
For patients unable to tolerate MRI, high-resolution CT scanning with and without contrast can be substituted.
Suspect acoustic neuroma in patients with unilateral sensorineural hearing loss. Tinnitus and dysequilibrium are also common complaints.
Initial testing should include audiometry. Brainstem evoked response audiometry can be used for further screening in patients with unexplained abnormalities.
Order MRI to confirm the diagnosis.
Treatment options include surgery, stereotactic radiosurgery, radiation, and observation. A
Refer patients for a multidisciplinary evaluation including a surgeon and radiation oncologist experienced in the management of vestibular schwannoma. B
A retrospective observational study of 169 patients undergoing excisional surgery for acoustic neuroma found no apparent benefit to a single dose of corticosteroids intra-operatively.

An RCT of 60 patients compared intra-operative ondansetron (4 mg IV given 30 minutes before case end) followed by oral ondansetron (8 mg bid) with placebo and found a significant reduction in post-operative nausea and vomiting with ondansetron.
A systematic review of 4 retrospective cohort studies found no benefit of aspirin for sporadic vestibular Schwannoma.
Have patients evaluated by an otologist and/or neurosurgeon experienced in vestibular schwannoma surgery.

The 3 main surgical approaches are the middle fossa, suboccipital, and translabyrinthine. The surgical approach is determined on the basis of the size of the tumor and the degree of preserved hearing.
The likelihood of long-term tumor control with microsurgical excision is 97% to 99%. Useful hearing can be preserved in 40% to 50% of cases.

A systematic review of 8 observational studies with 194 patients found that the overall rate of repeated stereotactic radiosurgery was 2.2%, with an average time between surgeries of just over 4 years.
Risk of operative mortality is low (1.1%). The most important long-term complications are hearing loss, facial weakness, facial numbness, and vestibular disturbances.

Risk of morbidity is related to tumor size, and even better rates of hearing preservation are possible with smaller tumors. Patients are unlikely to regain lost cranial nerve function regardless of the treatment option selected.

A review of patients with a median age of 64 years who underwent gamma knife radiosurgery (GKRS) reported a median tumor diameter of 17.5 mm and mean volume of 2.41 cm2; 51 of 52 experienced tumor control over a variable follow-up period 912 to 192 months). One patient required further surgery resulting in remission. Hearing loss (17%), ataxia (8%) and hydrocephalus (2%) were the most common complications.

Stereotactic radiosurgery (e.g., Cyberknife) delivers a single high-dose radiation treatment to a highly focal area. It is a well-established alternative to microsurgical excision for patients with tumors 0 to 3 cm in diameter. Ten-year tumor control rates of 97% have been reported with stereotactic radiosurgery. Hearing preservation rates of 40% to 70% have been reported with stereotactic radiosurgery.
Risks of treatment-related facial and trigeminal neuropathy are very low (<5%) with current radiosurgery techniques.

Radiosurgery carries a very low risk (<1%) of malignant transformation or a radiation-induced second malignancy. However, scarring following radiosurgery may make subsequent microsurgery difficult should the tumor recur.

Some have advocated longer treatment schedules using fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy as an alternative to radiosurgery to improve hearing preservation rates. A series of 154 patients receiving fractionated stereotactic radiotherapy in a reduced dose (46.8 Gy) achieved excellent tumor control and hearing preservation.

Careful observation may be an appropriate option for some patients. A large meta-analysis of more than 1300 patients showed a 57% rate of no growth after an average follow up of 3.2 years. For tumors with growth, the average growth rate was 1.9 mm/year. Hearing loss occurred in 51% of observed patients.

A randomized trial compared upfront radiosurgery with a wait and scan" approach. At 4 years the tumor volume reduction was greater with upfront radiosurgery. For most other outcomes there was no difference. Ultimately, 21 of 49 patients in the wait and scan group had radiosurgery.
Patients selected for observation should undergo follow-up MRIs at 6 months and then at yearly intervals.
Typically, untreated vestibular Schwannomas will grow 0 to 3 mm yearly. B
However, regression or tumor shrinkage of sporadic vestibular schwannomas may also occur in 6% to 13% of patients.
Both microsurgical resection and stereotactic radiosurgery offer high rates of tumor control and cranial nerve preservation. B

Surgical series report tumor control rates of 97% to 99%, functional hearing preservation in 48% of small tumors and 25% of medium tumors, and excellent facial nerve function preservation in 96% of small tumors, 74% of medium tumors, and 38% of large tumors. B
Radiosurgical series report 97% tumor control rates, hearing preservation rates of 50% to 77%, and new facial weakness rates of less than 1%. B

A multi-center study of 538 patients (mean age 64 years, 56% female, mean follow-up 8 years) found that 27% received microsurgery, 46% sterotactic radiosurgery, and the rest observation. Untreated patients were more likely to have headaches, and about half of all patients had headaches 8 years later. The likelihood of headache did not vary with the choice of active therapy.
Malignant transformation is rare, though.
